key_terms.meaning: A declarative sentence with exactly one truth value, true (T) or false (F); questions and commands are not propositions.
A table listing all 2ⁿ truth-value combinations of n propositional variables and the resulting value of the formula.
A formula true under every assignment of truth values to its variables; also called a universally valid formula.
A formula false under every assignment, such as p ∧ ¬p.
A formula that is true for some assignments and false for others.
Two formulas are equivalent (P ⇔ Q) when they have identical truth values in every row of the truth table.
The contrapositive of p → q is ¬q → ¬p; it is logically equivalent to the original implication.
A formula written as an OR of AND-clauses, each clause a conjunction of variables or their negations.
The OR of exactly those minterms for which the formula is true; also called sum of minterms.
The AND of exactly those maxterms for which the formula is false; also called product of maxterms.
A named argument form, such as modus ponens, that carries true premises to a true conclusion.
An argument whose conclusion is true whenever all its premises are true; validity is about form, not about actual truth.
A set of formulas that can all be true together under at least one truth assignment.
To prove P → Q, assume P as an extra premise, derive Q, and then discharge the assumption.
A statement P(x) containing variables; it becomes a proposition once the variables take values or are quantified.
The universal quantifier ∀x (for all x) and the existential quantifier ∃x (there exists an x).
The set of values the variables of a predicate may take; a quantified statement is meaningless without it.
Assume the negation of the claim, derive a falsehood such as r ∧ ¬r, and conclude the claim is true.
Prove P(base) and P(k) → P(k+1); then P(n) holds for all n in the stated range.
A refutation rule: from clauses (A ∨ p) and (B ∨ ¬p) derive (A ∨ B), aiming for the empty clause.

takeaways: A proposition has a truth value; connectives build bigger formulas whose values are read off a truth table.
Tautologies are the valid formulas, and every law of logic is the statement that some pair of formulas is equivalent.
An implication and its contrapositive say the same thing; the converse and inverse do not.
Any formula has a unique PDNF and PCNF up to ordering, and these are read directly from the truth table.
An argument is valid when its premises imply its conclusion; the truth of the conclusion alone never makes an argument valid.
Premises are consistent when some single assignment makes them all true; an inconsistent premise set implies anything.
Quantifiers turn predicates into propositions, and ∀ and ∃ obey De Morgan-style negation laws.
Direct, contrapositive, contradiction and induction are routes to the same claim; choose the one that gives you the easiest algebra.
Induction needs both the base case and the step; a missing or wrong base case breaks the whole proof.
Resolution finishes a proof by deriving the empty clause from the negated claim written in clause form.
bank_note: Long answers almost always pair a definition with a worked artefact — a filled truth table, a labelled derivation, a PDNF/PCNF pair or a complete induction — so the marks sit in the working, not in the wording.

bank.q: Define a proposition and list the five basic connectives (¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔) with their truth tables. Use truth tables to classify p → (q → p), p ∧ ¬p and (p → q) ∨ (q → p) as tautology, contradiction or contingency.
outline: Definition of proposition with two examples and two non-examples (question, command).
Truth tables for all five connectives, with 4 rows each for the binary ones.
Correct classification: first is a tautology, second a contradiction, third a tautology.
Statement that a contingency is neither, with one example such as p ∧ q.

bank.q: State the laws of logic — idempotent, commutative, associative, distributive, De Morgan, absorption, identity, domination and the implication law. Verify any two of them by truth table and use them to simplify a compound formula.
outline: Each law written as an equivalence, e.g. ¬(p ∧ q) ⇔ ¬p ∨ ¬q.
Implication law: p → q ⇔ ¬p ∨ q.
Truth tables for the two chosen laws, all rows matching.
Simplification chain showing each step and naming the law used.

bank.q: For the implication p → q, define the converse, inverse and contrapositive, and show by truth table which of them is equivalent to p → q. Give an everyday example of a statement and its contrapositive.
outline: Converse q → p, inverse ¬p → ¬q, contrapositive ¬q → ¬p.
Truth table showing p → q ⇔ ¬q → ¬p, and that converse and inverse are equivalent to each other only.
Clear example, e.g. 'if it rains, the ground is wet' and its contrapositive.
Warning that proving the converse does not prove the original.

bank.q: List eight rules of inference with their names and schematic forms. Define validity and explain why an argument can be valid while its conclusion is false.
outline: Modus ponens, modus tollens, disjunctive syllogism, hypothetical syllogism, simplification, conjunction, addition, constructive dilemma (or resolution).
Each written as premises over a line with the conclusion.
Validity defined as: premises all true forces conclusion true.
Example of a valid argument with a false premise and hence a false conclusion.

bank.q: For the formula f(p, q, r) = (p → q) ∧ (q → r), build the full truth table, then obtain its DNF, PDNF and PCNF. State how many minterms and maxterms it has.
outline: Eight-row truth table with the value of f in the last column.
Minterm for each true row, maxterm for each false row.
PDNF as the OR of the true-row minterms; PCNF as the AND of the false-row maxterms.
Remark that the number of minterms plus maxterms equals 2³.

bank.q: Test the validity of the following arguments using rules of inference: (a) 'If it rains, the ground is wet. The ground is not wet. Therefore it did not rain.' (b) p → q, q → r, ¬r, p ∨ s, therefore s.
outline: (a) Identified as modus tollens, reason stated.
(b) Derivation line by line: modus tollens on q → r and ¬r gives ¬q; modus tollens on p → q gives ¬p; disjunctive syllogism with p ∨ s gives s.
Each line labelled with the rule used and the lines it uses.
Conclusion: both arguments are valid.

bank.q: Use the CP rule (rule of conditional proof) to show that (p ∧ q) → r is a valid conclusion from the premise p → (q → r). Then explain what 'discharging the assumption' means.
outline: Assume p ∧ q as an extra premise.
Simplification gives p and q; modus ponens gives q → r and then r.
By CP, the assumption is discharged to yield p → (q → r).
Explanation that the derived line no longer depends on p ∧ q.

bank.q: Prove by mathematical induction: (a) 1² + 2² + … + n² = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 for all n ≥ 1; (b) 3^(2n+2) − 8n − 9 is divisible by 64 for all n ≥ 0.
outline: Base case for each with the arithmetic shown.
Inductive hypothesis stated clearly for n = k.
Step: add the (k+1)th term and simplify to the target formula; divisibility step writes the k+1 expression as 64m plus a multiple of 64.
Conclusion by the principle of induction.

bank.q: Use resolution to prove that (p → q) ∧ (q → r) ∧ p ∧ ¬r is unsatisfiable. Convert to clause form first, and show every resolvent.
outline: Rewrite implications as ¬p ∨ q and ¬q ∨ r; write the clause set.
Resolution steps: ¬p ∨ q with p gives q; q with ¬q ∨ r gives r; r with ¬r gives the empty clause.
Statement that the empty clause means the set is unsatisfiable.
Conclusion: the negation of the original claim being unsatisfiable proves the claim.

bank.q: Prove that √2 is irrational using proof by contradiction, and prove that if n² is odd then n is odd using proof by contraposition.
outline: Assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms; derive a² = 2b², so a is even, write a = 2m, get b even too.
Contradiction with 'lowest terms'.
Contrapositive: n even implies n² even, shown by n = 2m and squaring.
Conclusion covers both methods and states why contraposition works here.

bank.q: Symbolise the argument 'All students who attend every class pass. Ravi attends every class. Therefore Ravi passes.' using predicates and quantifiers, then establish validity using the rules of specification and generalization.
outline: Choose a universe and predicates: S(x) = x is a student, A(x) = attends every class, P(x) = passes.
Premises written as ∀x (S(x) ∧ A(x) → P(x)) and S(ravi) ∧ A(ravi).
Universal instantiation to Ravi, then modus ponens.
Clear statement of why the conclusion is a proposition and needs no generalization step here.

bank.q: An argument is given in English. Symbolise it, negate the conclusion, convert the whole set to clause form, and give a resolution refutation. Then comment on whether the original premises are consistent.
outline: Correct symbolisation with every atomic proposition listed.
Negated conclusion added, implications and biconditionals removed, formula in CNF.
Resolution chain ending in the empty clause, each resolvent shown.
Conclusion that the argument is valid.
Separate check that the premises alone have a satisfying assignment, so they are consistent.

bank.q: A 'proof' claims that n = n + 1 for all n, or that all horses are the same colour. Identify exactly where the induction argument fails and state what condition the principle of induction demands.
outline: Base case written out and checked.
Inductive step examined line by line; the hidden assumption or the wrong starting index found.
Statement that the step must work for every k in the range, not just some k.
Corrected version or statement that no proof exists.

bank.q: Distinguish consistency, inconsistency and validity. Given a set of premises that is inconsistent, show by the CP rule and the inconsistency rule that any conclusion follows, and explain why this makes such a premise set useless for reasoning.
outline: Definitions of consistent, inconsistent and valid, with one example each.
CP rule: assume the antecedent, derive the consequent, discharge.
Inconsistency rule: an inconsistency among premises yields any formula.
Evaluation: an inconsistent premise set entails everything, so it carries no information.

glossary.def: A symbol such as ¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔ that joins one or two propositions into a new proposition.
¬p, the proposition that is true exactly when p is false.
p ∧ q, true only when both p and q are true.
p ∨ q, true when at least one of p and q is true; in logic it is inclusive unless stated otherwise.
p → q, false only in the single case where p is true and q is false.
p ↔ q, true when p and q have the same truth value.
A formula built from variables, connectives and brackets by the syntax rules, so it has an unambiguous truth table.
The implication ¬q → ¬p, logically equivalent to p → q.
A conjunction containing each variable of the formula exactly once, either plain or negated; it is true in exactly one row of the truth table.
A disjunction containing each variable exactly once, plain or negated; it is false in exactly one row.
From p and p → q, infer q.
From ¬q and p → q, infer ¬p.
From p ∨ q and ¬p, infer q.
From p → q and q → r, infer p → r.
From ∀x P(x), infer P(c) for a particular element c of the universe.
From P(c) for an arbitrary element c, infer ∀x P(x).
A variable in a predicate that is not bound by any quantifier, so the formula is not yet a proposition.
A disjunction of literals; a formula in clause form is a conjunction of clauses, the input to resolution.
The clause (A ∨ B) obtained by resolving (A ∨ p) with (B ∨ ¬p).
The clause with no literals, always false; deriving it in resolution proves the clause set unsatisfiable.
The first value of n for which an induction proof checks P(n) directly.
A variant where the step assumes P(m) for all m ≤ k, not just P(k), to prove P(k+1).
The standard axioms for the natural numbers, including a successor function and the induction axiom schema.
A single case in which the claim fails, enough to disprove a universal statement.
A proof of p → q that shows p is false, so the implication is true regardless of q.
